html:
A feast held by the peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast, at which a host family gives away goods to its guests. The word comes from Chinook Jargon and means "to give".

A potlatch marked a birth, a naming, a marriage, a death or the raising of a totem pole. By accepting gifts, guests witnessed and confirmed the host's rank and rights to names, crests, songs and lands. Among the Kwakwaka'wakw, Tlingit, Haida, Nisga'a and Coast Salish, it was the centre of law and memory, made possible by the salmon and cedar wealth of the Northwest Coast.

Missionaries saw it as wasteful and heathen, and Canada banned it under the Indian Act from 1885 to 1951. In 1921 police broke up a large Kwakwaka'wakw potlatch, jailed people and seized their masks. Feasts went on in secret, and some of the seized regalia has since come home.
sum: A feast held by the peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast, at which a host family gives away goods to its guests. The word comes from Chinook Jargon and means "to give".
